drills.q: Explain how GCP's IAM policy evaluation model differs fundamentally from AWS's.
drills.a: AWS evaluates identity-based policies together with resource-based policies, with explicit Deny anywhere beating any Allow, plus permission boundaries and SCPs as outer ceilings. GCP binds roles onto a resource hierarchy (Organization -> Folder -> Project -> Resource) where the effective policy is the additive union of a resource's own bindings and everything inherited from ancestors -- a child cannot narrow or remove an ancestor's grant. The closest thing to explicit deny is a separate deny policy resource, not a clause inside the allow policy.

drills.q: A group has roles/editor bound at the org level. You need to revoke their access to one specific project. What are your real options?
drills.a: You cannot remove the inherited grant locally. Options: re-parent the project under a different folder/org node not covered by the binding; add a deny policy on the project blocking the specific permissions for that group; or (the real fix) narrow the org-level grant itself since a broad org-wide Editor binding was very likely wrong to begin with.

drills.q: What is a deny policy, how does it differ from an allow policy, and what are its limits?
drills.a: A distinct IAM v2 resource listing principals/permissions to block, evaluated at every hierarchy level, always winning over any allow grant regardless of which level it came from. Limits: 500 deny policies/resource, 500 deny rules/resource, 2,500 total principal appearances/resource, 12 logic operators per condition.

drills.q: Explain the difference between IAM and Organization Policy with a concrete example where both matter.
drills.a: IAM controls who can act by granting roles; it can't restrict configuration for everyone. Org Policy restricts configurations (e.g. no external IPs) platform-wide regardless of identity and grants nothing itself. Example: a project Owner has every IAM permission to attach an external IP, but if an org policy constraint denies external IPs at a parent folder, creation still fails -- both layers must permit the action.

drills.q: Walk through the Workload Identity Federation flow mechanically and name the misconfiguration that defeats it.
drills.a: An external token (GitHub OIDC, AWS STS, K8s SA, any OIDC/SAML) is presented to a workload identity pool provider; attribute mapping (CEL) maps claims to GCP attributes, and an attribute_condition (CEL) gates which tokens are accepted. On success, STS issues a short-lived federated token, typically used to impersonate a real service account. The defeating misconfiguration: omitting or under-scoping attribute_condition, so any subject the IdP will vouch for (any repo in the org, etc.) is accepted.

drills.q: State the hard limits on GCP custom roles and the practical consequence of hitting them.
drills.a: 300 custom roles per organization and 300 per project (independent caps), up to 3,000 permissions per role, 64KB combined size of title+description+permissions. Hitting the cap in a large org usually means teams created near-duplicate custom roles per team/project instead of sharing a smaller set -- fix via consolidation or scoping reusable roles at org level.

drills.q: Compare service account keys, attached identity, and Workload Identity Federation, and state when each is the right choice.
drills.a: Attached identity (Compute Engine/GKE/Cloud Run metadata server) is the default for workloads running on GCP compute -- no credential material at all. Workload Identity Federation is right for workloads outside GCP with an OIDC/SAML-capable identity (CI/CD, other clouds, on-prem). Static keys are the shrinking fallback only when neither applies -- long-lived, exportable, capped at 10 per service account with no built-in expiry.

drills.q: How would you configure cross-cloud Workload Identity Federation for AWS-hosted workloads without distributing GCP service account keys?
drills.a: Configure a workload identity pool provider of type AWS, which trusts AWS STS-signed GetCallerIdentity credentials from a specific AWS account, scoped further via the attribute condition to specific IAM roles. The AWS workload's existing IAM role credentials exchange for a short-lived GCP token with no GCP key material ever touching the AWS side.

drills.q: What is a Principal Access Boundary (PAB) policy and how does it differ from a deny policy?
drills.a: A PAB policy is a hard ceiling on the maximum resource scope a principal can ever access, regardless of what any current or future allow policy grants -- conceptually close to an AWS permission boundary. A deny policy blocks specific permissions rather than capping overall scope. Limits: 500 rules/policy, 10 policies bound per resource, 1,000 policies per org.

drills.q: Design the IAM structure for a company with three product teams, a shared platform team, and a compliance requirement that production payment data access be time-boxed and approved.
drills.a: One folder per product team containing that team's dev/staging/prod projects, plus a platform folder for shared infrastructure. Minimal org-level bindings (billing admin, org policy admin, a small break-glass Owner group). Payments-prod carries only read-only/operational standing role bindings; elevated write access goes through Privileged Access Manager entitlements -- time-boxed, approval-gated, auto-expiring, fully audited -- rather than any standing write grant.

drills.q: A workload identity pool provider's attribute condition was loosened during a migration and nobody noticed for three weeks. What's the blast radius and how do you detect this class of incident?
drills.a: Blast radius is every external caller the IdP itself considers valid for that provider -- e.g. any repo in the entire GitHub org, not just the intended one -- able to impersonate whichever service account the pool's bindings allow, for the whole exposure window. Detect via Cloud Audit Logs alerts on pool/provider config changes, plus runtime monitoring of STS token-exchange logs for unexpected source attribute values (e.g. a spike in distinct repository claims against a pool meant to serve one repo).
